historical_review.mathematical_justification: All 16 parents were read. Ideal-power quotients, prime quotients, polynomial-presentation quotients, square-zero quotients, and S_q/pS_q share the additive-coset construction with induced multiplication. Well-definedness follows because changing representatives by elements of an ideal changes sums/products by elements of that ideal. This is not an additive/module quotient alone: Z/2 as an additive quotient carries no general recipe for multiplying arbitrary quotient modules; the ring construction needs multiplication on the parent and an ideal. Quotients can be nonfields (Z/4), so the existing special field k[t]/(f) for irreducible f cannot resolve this general identity. Localization inverts a multiplicative set instead of killing an ideal. However occ.39767a08c003da7e344c in formally-smooth-ring-map has a compound context: an R-algebra, square-zero ideal, quotient algebra AND canonical quotient map, described as an extension. The underlying ring quotient is a justified shared prerequisite, but a whole square-zero extension datum is not identical to a quotient-ring object. Existing aliasing is not certified as equality of those compound objects by this review.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: The prime-ideal and Noetherian-module sources both refer to an associative commutative coefficient ring with identity. R versus A are bound variable renamings; module Noetherianity and primality impose separate restrictions not part of the ring axioms.

The locally-nilpotent-ideal and Jacobson-ring sources use commutative rings with multiplicative identity, just as the prime-ideal and Noetherian-module sources explicitly do. They share the associative commutative unital coefficient-ring prerequisite. Nilpotence, radical-ideal and Noetherian module restrictions remain separately attached to their parent statements.

The nonzero commutative unital ring R has associative commutative multiplication and a specified identity, exactly the general commutative unital ring prerequisite. Nonzeroness 0≠1 and field inversion, when present, remain parent-specific rather than imposed on all unital rings.

historical_review.mathematical_justification: All 11 parents were read. Five explicitly require an identity: commutative prime/maximal ideals, field, integral domain, and Noetherian module over a commutative ring with identity. Their additional properness, nonzeroness, invertibility or Noetherianity belongs to the parent, not to the bare ring candidate. Six Stacks-attributed paraphrases (nil ideal, both Jacobson-ring criteria, clopen spectrum, normal ring and irreducible spectrum components) say commutative ring without spelling out 1. As in the adopted adjudication policy, source attribution is not independent evidence of an ambient convention. Retain the recorded commutative-unital missing type, but defer exact source scope of those six uses; do not equate it with the existing identity-optional associative ring or certify the omitted unit hypothesis. Noncommutative 2x2 matrices show that having an identity does not force commutativity; the zero-product C2 rng shows commutativity alone need not give an identity. Z/4 is commutative unital but not an integral domain or field, so those stricter existing meanings are not generic resolutions. The zero ring question (whether 1=0 is permitted) must not inherit the field/domain parents nonzero condition accidentally.

The nilpotent-ideal source uses the positive integral ideal power I^n, and pure-ideal/completion sources use ideal multiplication IJ and its iterations I^n. Both depend on ordinary ideal multiplication in a ring, while the choice of n and nilpotence equation I^n=0 are parent hypotheses.

The Dedekind-domain factorization characterization requires a finite iterated product P_1⋯P_n of ideals with the same finite-sums-of-products construction as the binary ideal product IJ, including R as the empty product. The conditions that the factors are nonzero prime ideals, and that factorization is unique, belong only to the Dedekind characterization; aliasing does not make an arbitrary product prime or unique.

historical_review.mathematical_justification: Products are additive finite sums of factors ij with i∈I,j∈J; closure under left/right ring multiplication follows from the two-sided ideal axioms. Iterating gives positive powers, while I^0=R is an extra convention in the unital commutative contexts. IJ need not equal I∩J: in Z, (2)(2)=(4) whereas (2)∩(2)=(2); the purity parent imposes that equality as an extra test. Symbolic p^(n) is localization and contraction and is not ordinary p^n by definition. Five parents explicitly work in commutative-algebra/domain settings. However form.003cb1cc70cf5a2c.nilpotent-ideal, occ.6382ae14011d622d9352, has an identity-optional ring target and former candidate missing.28c2bfd6be87e9099167 with only Ring theory scope, whereas the canonical product requires commutative unital rings. Positive ideal powers also exist for nonunital rings: the nonzero zero-product C2 rng has I=R and I²=0. Thus the broader source reading is meaningful and is not covered as stated by the narrower canonical context. The construction is legitimate, but its alias scope needs adjudication; no generalization or split applied.

For a commutative unital algebra the chosen map k→A gives scalar multiplication c·a=φ(c)a and compatibility with multiplication; this extra data is not present in a bare commutative ring. A=k[T] is a k-algebra but not a field, and A=k[ε]/(ε²) is a k-algebra but is not reduced or a domain, separating the underlying type from the geometric tests. A field extension is narrower (A must itself be a field), while finite-presentation algebra imposes finite generators and relations. The existing unital ring-map meaning describes the structure arrow rather than the whole algebra object. However all five actual source texts say k-algebra, without independently spelling out commutativity and the unit axiom. Their commutative-algebra/ring-spectrum context supports the intended reading but does not independently certify external conventions. Retain the missing structured type and document precise source verification instead of declaring the specialized assumptions proved.

form.wave2.foundation.tagged-riemann-int.display_term: proper Riemann integral on a compact interval
form.wave2.foundation.tagged-riemann-int.text: Let f:[a,b]→R be bounded with a<b. For a finite partition a=x_0<⋯<x_n=b and arbitrary tags ξ_i∈[x_{i−1},x_i], let S=Σ_{i=1}^n f(ξ_i)(x_i−x_{i−1}) and mesh=max_i(x_i−x_{i−1}). The function f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] with integral L∈R if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that |S−L|<ε for every tagged partition with mesh<δ.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: Discrete-time and real-time martingale definitions both use L^1 integrability of each real random variable, E|X_t|<∞; the index symbol and its range (natural vs nonnegative real time) do not alter the integrability predicate. Filtration and martingale equalities remain separate.

Conditional expectation requires integrable real X and Z, namely E|X|<∞ and E|Z|<∞. Continuous-time and discrete-time martingale formulations require exactly the L¹ integrability predicate for each real random variable X_t. Time indexing and conditional-expectation criteria stay parent-specific.

The original second discrete-time martingale variant states its process (X_n,F_n) is integrable, which means E|X_n|<∞ for each n≥0. The first discrete-time and continuous-time martingale formulations explicitly state E|X_t|<∞ at each index, without requiring a common bound, and the conditional-expectation source also uses integrability as finite absolute expectation. The sole shared prerequisite is coordinatewise L¹ integrability for a real random variable at each time parameter; specializing its index set T from nonnegative reals to nonnegative integers gives precisely the discrete-time condition. The process index set, adaptation, filtration, conditional expectation identities, and absence of a uniform L¹ bound remain specified in their respective full source formulations.

historical_review.mathematical_justification: All four sources legitimately need L¹-integrability of each indicated real random variable, ∫|X|dP<∞. Measurability alone is insufficient: on Ω={1,2,...} with P({k})=2^(−k), Z(k)=2^k is real-valued and measurable but E|Z|=Σ1=∞. Individual integrability imposes no common bound: deterministic X_n=n has E|X_n|=n finite for each n. However the canonical stored context literally says for every REAL time t≥0 in a stochastic process, whereas the conditional-expectation parent has two individual variables X,Z and the other two parents have integer-time sequences. The historical alias reasons intend the common single-variable L¹ prerequisite, but their whole predicates are not equivalent: set Y_t=0 at integer times and Y_t=Z above at noninteger times; all integer coordinates are integrable but not all real coordinates. Thus sharing the local predicate is justified, while identifying the full real-index process requirement with the other inputs is not. A candidate-context granularity/quantifier clarification is needed; no generalization or split is applied.

form.wave2.foundation.topological-space.text: A topological space is a pair (X,τ) with τ⊆P(X) such that ∅∈τ and X∈τ, any union of members of τ is in τ, and intersections of finitely many members of τ are in τ. Members of τ are the open subsets of X.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: Two connected-space formulations both reference a clopen subset of X, meaning a subset of X simultaneously open and closed. The nonemptiness assumption in one connectedness variant is separate from this common subset property.

The connected-space and connected-topological-space variants both refer to a subset of a fixed topological space simultaneously open and closed in that ambient topology. The parent connectedness statements differ on whether the empty space is admitted; clopen does not resolve that discrepancy.

historical_review.mathematical_justification: In every source the needed local predicate is U open in X AND X\U open in X. It is meaningful for arbitrary spaces, including empty X, where ∅=X is the only clopen. A nonempty space is connected iff no nontrivial clopen occurs: such a clopen gives the two disjoint nonempty opens U and X\U, and a separation makes either half clopen. This shared predicate does not decide whether the parent convention excludes empty spaces. The existing clopen-spectrum meaning is the idempotent correspondence, not the bare predicate: in Spec(R), idempotent e gives D(e)=V(1−e), but generic topology supplies no ring element. The canonical candidate context explicitly fixes U⊆Spec(R) while calling it an instance of the generic clopen predicate; its two aliased contexts and three connectedness parents instead use arbitrary X. Hence the common underlying predicate is mathematically justified, but the canonical ambient restriction versus polymorphic intent needs clarification. No arbitrary topological X is assumed to be a prime spectrum, and no idempotent data are transferred to it.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: For any field k and nonconstant irreducible f∈k[x], the canonical quotient k[x]/(f) is a field and α=x+(f) satisfies f(α)=0 by the quotient relation. Thus the phrase 'class of x as a root of f' instantiates the same contextual root concept as an arbitrary polynomial zero in an extension field. The quotient construction and choice of α remain extra source details. Repeated roots and monic polynomials are separate concepts.

Splitting fields and irreducible-polynomial quotient fields each use a root α of a polynomial over a smaller field in an extension, meaning polynomial evaluation equals zero. Root multiplicity, splitting and field generation remain parent-specific.

In the algebraically closed field source, a root a∈K of a nonconstant polynomial f∈K[x] means f(a)=0. In the irreducible polynomial quotient, splitting-field and separable-degree sources, a root α in a field extension E/F means f(α)=0 after coefficient inclusion. The first is precisely the K=F=E special case of the second polynomial-root prerequisite. Neither is confused with a root of unity or a field radical.

historical_review.mathematical_justification: All four parents use f(α)=0 in a specified extension field; the quotient-field parent correctly assumes irreducible f, so the residue class of x is a root. Roots are elements, not evaluation homomorphisms, whole splitting fields, or root multiplicities. A root need not be a root of unity (0 roots T), and T² has one distinct root despite degree two. A canonical-context defect remains: it says K=F[x]/(f) for nonconstant f without requiring irreducibility. F[T]/(T²) has a nonzero nilpotent T-class and is not a field, although that class satisfies the equation. The generic field-root prerequisite is sound in these sources; the abbreviated quotient example needs the irreducibility qualification. Proposed clarification NOT APPLIED.

historical_review.mathematical_justification: All three denominator occurrences invoke multiplication-closed S. The recorded candidate additionally contains 1_R. In a unital ring the nonzerodivisors contain 1 and are closed: if abx=0 and a,b are regular, first bx=0 then x=0. But all three stored formulations omit an explicit unit axiom, and the effective generic ring targets allow no identity. Multiplicative closure alone does not produce a unit: {0} is closed in Z but does not contain 1. Neither does a bare subset define a localization or require denominators be regular; the canonical context does not exclude 0, so no such exclusion is invented. Retain the unital multiplicative-set type while deferring the exact source conventions rather than certifying narrower hypotheses.

form.wave2.module94.unital-left-module.text: Let R be a ring with identity 1 and let (M,+) be an abelian group. A unital left R-module is an action R×M→M satisfying r(m+n)=rm+rn, (r+s)m=rm+sm, (rs)m=r(sm), and 1m=m for all r,s∈R and m,n∈M.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: For a commutative ring R, the submodule IM is generated by products i·m; taking the ideal I^n instead of I yields (I^n)M as a special instance of the same general ideal-action-on-module construction. Ideal multiplication and forming quotient modules remain separate. Compared the entire source for 'submodule IM generated by products I·M' against canonical candidate 'I^n M'; source phrasing remains immutable.

historical_review.mathematical_justification: Finite sums Σi_jm_j form a submodule: addition concatenates sums, negatives can be absorbed in the ideal, and r(i_jm_j)=(ri_j)m_j remains of the same form. This differs from ideal multiplication, whose outputs lie in R, and from M/IM, whose elements are cosets. Taking I^n specializes the same ideal action. For unital M, RM=M; a ring identity alone does not force this for broad actions (the zero-action C₂ module over F₂ has RM=0). The canonical type restricts R to commutative unital, while the three paraphrases leave ambient conventions implicit; current module targets use the unital specialization. Positive ideal powers are meaningful more generally, but that does not authorize broadening this canonical type or applying I^0M=M universally.

form.wave2.module94.unital-left-module.text: Let R be a ring with identity 1 and let (M,+) be an abelian group. A unital left R-module is an action R×M→M satisfying r(m+n)=rm+rn, (r+s)m=rm+sm, (rs)m=r(sm), and 1m=m for all r,s∈R and m,n∈M.

form.wave2.foundation.field-commutative-.text: A field is a commutative ring k with identity 1_k, with 0≠1_k, such that for every a∈k with a≠0 there exists b∈k satisfying ab=1_k (and hence ba=1_k).

form.wave2.foundation.orthogonality-meas.text: Let μ be a nonnegative Borel or Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure on a real interval (a,b) and let n be a nonnegative integer such that x↦x^n is μ-integrable. The nth raw moment of μ is μ_n=∫_a^b x^n dμ(x). It is finite only when the integral is finite.

form.wave2.foundation.tagged-riemann-int.text: Let f:[a,b]→R be bounded with a<b. For a finite partition a=x_0<⋯<x_n=b and arbitrary tags ξ_i∈[x_{i−1},x_i], let S=Σ_{i=1}^n f(ξ_i)(x_i−x_{i−1}) and mesh=max_i(x_i−x_{i−1}). The function f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] with integral L∈R if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that |S−L|<ε for every tagged partition with mesh<δ.

historical_review.mathematical_justification: The Lebesgue integral is a construction using a measurable integrand and measure, not a raw-moment name alone or a Riemann integral under arbitrary tags. Here the integrand is specifically x^n and finite L1 integrability is supplied, so its value is exactly the parent raw moment. form.wave2.analysis.orthogonal-polynomia.text: Let μ be a nonnegative Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure arising from an admissible bounded nondecreasing function with infinitely many points of increase and finite moments ∫|x|^k dμ(x)<∞ for all integers k≥0. A polynomial family p_n of degree n is orthogonal with respect to μ when ∫p_n(x)p_m(x)dμ(x)=0 for n≠m.

historical_review.mathematical_justification: The source uses infinitely many points of increase to exclude finite-support degeneration, but neither the short formulation nor its stored observation specifies a precise one-sided/local definition of point of increase. It must not be replaced by strict monotonicity everywhere: an atomic distribution with infinitely many jumps is not strictly increasing between jumps. Conversely, if the measure has only finitely many support points a_i, the nonzero polynomial product(X−a_i) vanishes in its L2 seminorm, preventing positive norms in every degree. Connecting the generator wording to support requires the Stieltjes normalization and endpoint convention already deferred at rank166.

historical_review.mathematical_justification: A fundamental system at x consists of connected neighborhoods cofinal inside ALL neighborhoods of x, not merely a cover of X by connected sets. The individual neighborhoods need not be open. A global topology basis contains open sets throughout the space and need not be a neighborhood system at one point, so occ.cdc96f16a3e31332ec7d is not a direct identity with this datum. There is a legitimate related theorem: if every point has the stated system, each connected component of an open U is open, because each of its points has a connected neighborhood inside U contained in that component. This yields a global connected-open basis, but it is a derived characterization requiring explanation.

form.7ca4fb934b2f076c.r-derivation.text: For a ring map R→S and an S-module M, an R-derivation D:S→M is an additive map vanishing on the image of R and satisfying Leibniz's law D(ab)=aD(b)+bD(a).

Wedge multiplication adds differential graded algebra structure beyond a bare cochain complex. The candidate leaves the module base unstated and must retain this ambiguity.

form.a9ca2e716ceffd36.support-module.text: For an R-module M, its support Supp_R(M) is the subset {p∈Spec(R):M_p≠0} of the prime spectrum, where M_p denotes localization at p.

Localizing M at precisely this subset gives M_p, an R_p-module, and support tests whether THIS object is zero. A generic multiplicative subset does not determine a prime complement, and R_p as a ring is not an arbitrary localized module. The candidate combines the subset construction with a specialization of an existing localization construction, so no entire-object identity with the multiplicative-subset candidate alone is justified.

form.988d26ef7c849694.epimorphism-commut.text: A ring homomorphism f:R→S is an epimorphism in the category of commutative rings if every pair of ring maps g,h:S→T satisfying g∘f=h∘f are equal; equivalently the multiplication map S⊗_R S→S is an isomorphism.

descriptor.context: Category theory: epimorphism

form.eed0c34725956bb5.categorical-epimor.text: A morphism f:X→Y in a category C is an epimorphism if for every object W and maps a,b:Y→W, equality a∘f=b∘f implies a=b.

historical_review.mathematical_justification: The canonical multiplication map mu(s tensor t)=st uses the commutative R-algebra tensor product, not just its underlying module or an arbitrary ring isomorphism. If f is epi, the two canonical maps i1,i2:S→S tensor_R S agree since they agree on R; then s tensor t=i1(s)i2(t)=i1(st), proving mu inverse to i1. Conversely if mu is invertible then i1=i2, and maps g,h agreeing on R induce s tensor t↦g(s)h(t), forcing g=h. Epimorphism is not set-surjectivity: Z→Q is epi because any extension of a unital map must send a/b to the unique g(a)g(b)^−1, but it is not onto. The candidate phrase bundles the map and its isomorphism criterion; neither should be resolved to the whole parent or generic isomorphism without segmentation.

source.display_term: derivation relative to a base ring
source.context: Commutative algebra: derivation relative to a base ring
source.text: For a ring map R→S and an S-module M, an R-derivation D:S→M is an additive map vanishing on the image of R and satisfying Leibniz's law D(ab)=aD(b)+bD(a).

references.phrase: D vanishes on image of R
references.disposition: The derivation is R-relative; this restriction is stronger than additivity alone.
This Leibniz identity is the defining multiplicative compatibility, not multiplicativity of D.

source.context: Commutative algebra: quasi-regular sequence relative to a module

references.reason: The graded comparison needs both the coefficient quotient ring and induced quotient module.

references.context: Commutative algebra: polynomial algebra R[X_i : i in I] over a commutative unital coefficient ring R, for an arbitrary set I of independent indeterminates; each polynomial has finite monomial support. source.context: Module theory: finitely generated module
source.text: An R-module M is finitely generated if there exist m_1,…,m_n∈M such that M=Rm_1+⋯+Rm_n; equivalently there is a surjective homomorphism R^n→M for some finite n.

references.context: Module theory: submodule generated by a subset S of a left R-module M, consisting of all finite R-linear combinations of elements of S; for a finite S={m_1,...,m_n} this is the finite R-linear span Σ_i R m_i, possibly all of M.
references.matching_note: The span is the submodule comprising R-linear combinations of chosen generators; the further equality with M is the source's finite-generation condition, not part of the general generated-submodule definition.

references.context: Set theory: surjective function f:X→Y whose image is the entire stated codomain Y; for module homomorphisms this is the underlying-set surjectivity of the R-linear map, independent of linearity, free domain, or choice of basis.
references.matching_note: The R-linear map's surjectivity refers to the underlying set mapping onto its stated codomain; the module-linearity and free-domain conditions remain separate source dependencies.

references.context: Module theory: finite-rank free left R-module R^n over a unital ring R for finite n≥0, the direct sum of n copies of the regular left R-module, with its canonical standard basis; not the same as an arbitrary locally free module.
references.matching_note: The finite direct sum R^n is the finite-rank free module, not merely a finitely generated module or a locally free module. The rank or multiplicity n remains part of each source.

references.disposition: The generator count is finite but does not imply the module has finitely many elements.

source.context: Commutative algebra: Henselian local ring
source.text: A local ring (R,m) with residue field κ is Henselian if every monic f∈R[T] and every simple zero ā of f̄ in κ lift to a zero a∈R reducing to ā modulo m.

references.context: Commutative algebra and algebraic geometry: residue field A/m of a commutative local ring (A,m), including the prime-localized κ(p)=R_p/pR_p and the scheme-point κ(s)=O_{S,s}/m_s.
references.matching_note: Original phrase 'residue field κ=R/m' denotes quotient by the maximal ideal of a local ring, including the localized-at-prime and scheme-stalk cases; not an arbitrary extension field.
references.phrase: residue field of a local ring

references.context: Polynomial algebra: a nonzero univariate polynomial f(X)=a_nX^n+⋯+a_0 over a commutative unital coefficient ring is monic if its leading coefficient a_n equals the multiplicative identity 1, including degree zero unit polynomial 1.
references.matching_note: The leading polynomial coefficient is the multiplicative identity; residue field and Hensel lifting properties remain distinct.

references.context: Polynomial algebra over a field: a simple root α of f in a field extension means f(α)=0 and f'(α)≠0, equivalently (x−α)^2 does not divide f over that extension field. For reduction modulo a maximal ideal the root and derivative are taken in the residue field.
references.matching_note: The reduction polynomial has derivative nonzero at its root in the residue field, making it simple rather than repeated.

references.disposition: Lifting a simple root of the reduced monic polynomial to a root in R with the specified residue is exactly the Henselian root-lifting condition defined here; residue field, simple roots and monic polynomials are already separately classified.

references.disposition: The quantifiers range over all eligible pairs; multiple roots in κ are not covered by this simple-root criterion.

obs.wave2.cross109.linear-transformation.context: Field-vector-space linear map preserving linear combinations / one-combined-linearity-law
obs.wave2.cross109.linear-transformation.editorial_note: The source distinguishes R-linear maps of modules from the field-vector-space specialization. The general form needs additive homomorphism and compatibility with the same left R-scalar action on domain/codomain. Its vector version combines the two laws into one (the usual equivalence follows from T(0)=0). Field vector spaces are unital modules over K, but general R-modules need not be field vector spaces. The source also defines linear operator as a linear map from a module to itself; that is a specialization of domain/codomain, not a third inequivalent general definition. Be cautious that a noncommutative division-ring vector version requires compatible LEFT actions; our admitted field version explicitly restricts scalars to commutative K. No bijection, continuity, injectivity, surjectivity or finite-dimensionality is implied. Sections: General R-module definition, Definition in a Vector Space, Linear Operator scope distinguished

source.display_term: proper Riemann integral on a compact interval
source.context: Classical real analysis: universal sufficiently fine tagged partition integral
source.text: Let f:[a,b]→R be bounded with a<b. For a finite partition a=x_0<⋯<x_n=b and arbitrary tags ξ_i∈[x_{i−1},x_i], let S=Σ_{i=1}^n f(ξ_i)(x_i−x_{i−1}) and mesh=max_i(x_i−x_{i−1}). The function f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] with integral L∈R if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that |S−L|<ε for every tagged partition with mesh<δ.

Equality is almost sure, not pointwise. This meaning is scoped to real-valued integrable adapted sequences and integer time, not continuous-index processes or local martingales. Both formulations go under the same contextual meaning. Source section: Definition 1
obs.wave2.research80.martingale-discrete.text: A real-valued discrete-time process (X_n)_{n≥0}, adapted to a filtration (F_n)_{n≥0} and satisfying E|X_n|<∞ for every n, is a martingale if E[X_{n+1}|F_n]=X_n almost surely for each n≥0.

obs.wave2.group115.set-partition.02.editorial_note: ProofWiki supplies two equivalent definitions of an UNINDEXED set partition: pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets covering S, and exactly one block containing each point. Both permit an infinite set or infinite collection of blocks; no finite cardinality constraint is added. In particular, for S=∅ the empty collection is the unique partition, since nonempty-block and pointwise conditions are vacuous. The page additionally distinguishes an indexed partitioning (family indexed by an I) from the partition as the resulting set of distinct blocks; the source's indexed alternative is not merged as an identical data structure. These definitions do not assume an ordering on the blocks and do not give an equivalence relation directly, though partitions induce such a relation. A family permitting empty blocks is not a partition under the source's explicit convention. Source sections: Definition 1 pairwise disjoint, cover and nonempty blocks, Definition 2 each element belongs to exactly one nonempty block, Indexed partitioning distinguished

obs.wave2.conv125.eigenvector-operator.0.editorial_note: The source explicitly states both a nonzero vector lying in the kernel of A−λI and equivalently Av=λv. These are the SAME eigenvector meaning for a linear endomorphism over a common field K because (A−λI)v=0 is equivalent to Av=λv. Crucial nonzero condition: the zero vector always satisfies Av=λv, but it is NOT an eigenvector, so an eigenvector is a nonzero element of the eigenspace. A is a linear OPERATOR V→V, not an arbitrary linear transformation V→W with incomparable input/output for λI. The page assumes λ is already an eigenvalue rather than defining that term; no eigenvalue-target link may be invented if its mathematical source meaning is unavailable. The full kernel ker(A−λI) is an eigenspace and contains 0; do not conflate eigenspace and set of eigenvectors. 'Eigenfunction' applies in specialized function-space contexts and is not blindly synonymous for every abstract vector eigenvector. No finite dimensionality requirement is implied. Sections: Definition nonzero kernel criterion, Equivalent eigen-equation, Eigenspace separate concept
